claims.text: In dual-phase high-entropy alloys, stress-induced in situ phase transformation can provide the dominant contribution to strain hardening and benefit both strength and ductility.
Mechanical loading produces stacking-fault networks in the fcc matrix.
The stacking-fault networks seed a local fcc-to-hcp transformation.
A twin-mediated transformation can serve as an alternative to the fcc-to-hcp transformation in the proposed mechanism.
The transformation supplies additional strain hardening while accommodating plastic deformation.
The relevant initial materials are equiatomic or near-equiatomic, single-phase fcc CrCoNi-based or Cantor-like HEAs.
The relevant initial alloys possess significant lattice distortion and low stacking-fault energy.
Lowering stacking-fault energy promotes TRIP or twinning, whereas raising stacking-fault energy suppresses these responses.
Fluctuations associated with lattice distortion and compositional inhomogeneity lower the energy barrier for stacking-fault formation.
Concentration-wave-associated fluctuations in lattice friction intrinsically promote the formation of stacking-fault networks.
The resulting transformation or twinning impedes dislocation motion.
An HEA with active TRIP or twinning will have a higher strain-hardening rate than a transformation-suppressed baseline.
An HEA with active TRIP or twinning will have a higher yield strength than a transformation-suppressed baseline.
An HEA with active TRIP or twinning will exhibit greater uniform elongation than a transformation-suppressed baseline.
Deformation of the active alloy will produce a detectable hcp phase or twin network.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to transformation-capable HEAs with substantial lattice distortion and low intrinsic stacking-fault energy.
The mechanism may not operate in high-stacking-fault-energy alloys or compositions that do not support a stress-driven phase change.
The hcp product phase can be intrinsically stronger but less ductile or tough than the fcc phase.
The balance between transformation hardening and product-phase brittleness may vary with temperature, strain rate, and composition.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and boundary describe dual-phase HEAs as the target system, whereas the stated initial material is single-phase fcc. The text does not clarify whether the second phase is present initially or generated only during deformation.
